one_liner: Loop-unrolled, batch-tempered MT19937 in one C++ file; same output as reference mt19937ar.c, 1.1-1.6x faster on Intel.
what_it_does: A two-file (mersenne-twister.h/.cpp) implementation of 32-bit MT19937 that produces the same sequence as the Matsumoto/Nishimura reference; test-mt checks 2000 consecutive outputs and outputs at doubling indices up to ~4 billion against it. The API is two extern "C" functions on a hidden singleton: seed(uint32_t) and rand_u32(). It is not a std::mt19937-style class and has no 64-bit variant.
how_it_is_fast: The state-update loop is split into two index ranges (0..226 and 227..622) so the wrap-around modulus disappears, the odd/even matrix select uses a branchless sign-extension trick ((int32_t(y) << 31) >> 31) & MAGIC instead of a table lookup, and tempering is done for all 624 words in one batch into a second array so rand_u32() is just an array read. The Makefile adds -O2 -march=native -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize so the batch loops can vectorize.
when_to_use: Legacy code that must keep the exact MT19937 sequence (reproducible simulations, saved seeds) but wants a faster scalar implementation than mt19937ar.c
C or C++ projects on x86 that want a tiny vendorable MT19937 with no dependencies
Single-threaded Monte Carlo code drawing many 32-bit values in a tight loop
when_not_to_use: Multithreaded code: state is one static global struct with no locking; you must edit the source to make it per-instance
When you are free to change generator: modern generators (lehmer64, wyrand, splitmix64, pcg64) are faster and MT19937 fails PractRand binary-rank tests
Non-Intel CPUs: the author says he only tested Intel and doubts the speedup holds elsewhere; the extra unrolling (MT_UNROLL_MORE) is slower on newer Xeons
Code already using std::mt19937: no comparison against libstdc++/libc++ is published, and those implementations may already be competitive
Need for 64-bit outputs, jump-ahead, or cryptographic unpredictability (624 outputs reveal the state, per the README)

integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (Makefile uses --std=gnu++11; source uses default member initializers)
integration.platforms: any in principle; only tested on Intel x86-64
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: single static MTState shared by all callers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same output sequence as mt19937ar.c's init_genrand/genrand_int32, but different function names (seed/rand_u32) and no init_by_array or real-valued outputs

gotchas: Exports unprefixed C symbols named seed and rand_u32, which can collide with other code; the README's namespace wrapper does not change the extern "C" linkage names
Earlier unrolled versions produced wrong numbers and had an out-of-bounds read (both fixed per README); the srand/rand drop-ins were removed because the author believed they had errors
State is ~5 KB (624 raw + 624 tempered words), double the reference's footprint
No LICENSE file in the repo; the BSD license is stated only in the README and source headers
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this only when you must keep the MT19937 sequence; if the generator can change, testingRNG's lehmer64 or wyrand headers are about 2x faster than MT19937 in that repo's table, and SHISHUA or xoshiro8x256pp are far faster for bulk fills.
verified_claims_summary: Author's own test-mt run (best of 20 passes, both implementations built with the repo Makefile's -O2 -march=native flags) gave 351-355 M numbers/s vs 222-223 M/s for the reference mt19937ar code (1.59x) on an unnamed Intel Xeon with gcc 6.3, and only 1.12x on an older Core i7 with clang 4; no comparison with std::mt19937.
status_note: Abandoned since December 2017, but it is two small BSD-licensed files (license stated in README only) that are easy to vendor.
